claims.text: Deliberate compositional modifications in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-based alloys produce variations in stacking fault energy.
Stacking fault energy governs the balance between deformation twinning and dislocation slip.
The balance between deformation twinning and dislocation slip dictates mechanical-property differences relative to equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Composition can be systematically modified to tune stacking fault energy.
Stacking fault energy determines the relative ease of twin formation versus dislocation glide.
Composition-induced changes in stacking fault energy modify the energy barrier for dislocation motion.
Lower stacking fault energy promotes deformation twinning.
Lower stacking fault energy induces serrated flow.
Lower stacking fault energy enhances work hardening.
Lower stacking fault energy can enhance ductility.
Higher stacking fault energy favors conventional dislocation slip.
Higher stacking fault energy decreases deformation-twinning activity.
Alloys with lower stacking fault energy will begin deformation twinning earlier than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Alloys with lower stacking fault energy will exhibit more pronounced serrated flow than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
The effects attributed to lower stacking fault energy will be particularly pronounced under cryogenic conditions.
Alloys with higher stacking fault energy will have fewer deformation twins and a lower hardening rate than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies to comparable single-phase FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloys and their lower-complexity subsets.
Differences in phase stability or grain-size distribution may prevent the proposed mechanism from extending to other alloys.
Solute-dislocation interactions may confound attempts to isolate the mechanical effects of stacking fault energy.
Processing history may change the quantitative effect of stacking fault energy on deformation mechanisms.

contradictions.description: The initial-state description permits substitution with an unspecified less expensive element, which could place an alloy outside the Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system, whereas the boundary restricts the hypothesis to that system and its lower-complexity subsets.
